title: Plaited stitch
subtitle: A Victorian twisted-stitch technique that produces a firm, rope-like fabric.
excerpt: Plaited stitch works every knit stitch through the back loop, producing a fabric of twisted columns that is denser and more structured than standard stocking stitch. It appears throughout Victorian knitting manuals as a foundation for heavy-wear garments and is considered an ancestor of modern cable work.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, Series 1 (1886), describes plaited knitting as working the stitch through the back loop for a firm, hard-wearing fabric. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) discusses the plaited stitch family in the context of traditional European knitting.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a swatch in plaited stitch, showing the distinctive twisted vertical columns of tightly worked stocking stitch.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitting technique in which every knit stitch is worked through the back loop, producing a twisted column and a firm, dense fabric. Used in Victorian-era garments for durability.
To insert the needle into the back leg of the stitch on the left needle rather than the front, and knit as normal. Abbreviated k1tbl. The resulting stitch is twisted and sits at a slight angle.

content.text: is an older name for working every knit stitch

(k1tbl) across right-side rows, while the wrong-side rows are purled normally. The effect is a fabric of distinctly twisted knit columns that read as a tight, rope-like texture. Victorian pattern manuals used this method throughout for its durability and neat appearance on garments knitted in fine wool. It is harder on the hands than plain stocking stitch, and slightly slower to work, but produces a crisper fabric. Difficulty: intermediate.
DK or 4-ply yarn in any fibre
Needles one size smaller than you would normally use for the yarn weight (the twist tightens the fabric)
Cast on any number of stitches using your preferred cast-on method.

Row 1 (RS): Insert the needle into the back leg of the first stitch on the left needle. Wrap the yarn and draw a new loop through. Slide the stitch off the left needle. Repeat across the row (k1tbl across).
Row 2 (WS): Purl every stitch in the normal way through the front loop (p across).
Repeat rows 1 and 2 for the body of the piece.

attrs.title: Continental knitters
attrs.body: When picking the yarn rather than throwing, working through the back loop requires a slightly different needle angle. Many Continental-style knitters find that a correctly mounted stitch (right leg forward on the needle) worked through the front loop gives the same result as working through the back of a conventionally mounted stitch. Experiment with a small swatch to confirm.

content.text: Plaited stitch appears in historical reproductions of Victorian garments, in hard-wearing accessories such as knitted bags and heavy socks, and as a surface texture in modern pattern design. A single column of plaited stitches between two knit columns reads as a clean, subtle cable alternative. The stitch is also the direct ancestor of simple cable work, where groups of twisted stitches are crossed against each other.

items.symptom: The fabric is tighter than expected and the gauge is off
items.cause: The twist compresses the stitch; the fabric always runs smaller than standard stocking stitch
items.fix: Work a gauge swatch in plaited stitch specifically, not in standard stocking stitch. Go up a needle size if the swatch runs tight against the pattern gauge.

items.symptom: The stitches feel stiff and hard to work through the back loop
items.cause: The previous row's purl stitches are sitting twisted on the needle
items.fix: Check that purl stitches on wrong-side rows are worked through the front leg. A twisted purl stitch will mount the wrong way on the needle, making the next k1tbl very tight.

items.symptom: Only some stitches look twisted; others look plain
items.cause: Some stitches were knitted through the front loop by mistake
items.fix: On right-side rows, check that the needle enters through the back of every stitch before the yarn is thrown.
